notes.title: Bangla drops "is" in the present
notes.body:
There is no present-tense "is/are" linking two nouns. **এটা আমার বই** is literally "this my book" — and that is the complete, correct sentence.

আছে is a different verb meaning "exists / is present", used for location and possession, not for identity.

notes.title: The verb goes last
notes.body:
Bangla is subject–object–verb. **আমি ভাত খাই** is "I rice eat".

Once you expect the verb at the end, long sentences stop feeling scrambled — everything before it is setup.

notes.title: Three words for "you"
notes.body:
Bangla grades politeness into the pronoun itself:

- **আপনি** — polite. Elders, strangers, anyone senior.
- **তুমি** — familiar. Friends, peers, younger family.
- **তুই** — intimate. Close childhood friends and siblings; rude to the wrong person.

The verb ending changes to match: আপনি করেন / তুমি কর / তুই করিস.

notes.title: কি versus কী
notes.body:
Same sound, two jobs, and the spelling distinguishes them:

- **কি** turns a statement into a yes/no question. *তুমি কি ভাত খাবে?* — "Will you eat rice?"
- **কী** means "what". *তোমার নাম কী?* — "What is your name?"

Many native writers blur these, so expect to see both.

notes.title: পানি or জল — where you are matters
notes.body:
Bangladesh says **পানি** for water; West Bengal says **জল**. Both are correct Bangla, and the choice quietly signals where you learned it.

This course teaches the Bangladeshi form throughout. Other pairs like this: নুন/লবণ (salt), and the greetings আসসালামু আলাইকুম versus নমস্কার.

notes.title: The -টা ending
notes.body:
Bangla attaches a *classifier* to make a noun definite. **বই** is "a book"; **বইটা** is "the book".

Use টা for most things, জন for people (তিনজন মানুষ — three people), and খানা for flat objects.
